EDUCATION & TRAINING

I hold a technical diploma in software development from CECyT 9, part of Mexico’s National Polytechnic Institute (IPN).

After studying computer systems engineering at ESCOM-IPN, I am now pursuing a degree in bionic engineering at UPIITA, IPN’s interdisciplinary campus for advanced technologies. My academic focus is biorobotics, particularly soft robotics.

I also hold a diploma in cybercrime and fraud investigation from the Mexican Institute of Criminal Investigation (IMIC). My interests in security include cryptography, web application security, protocol analysis, and reverse engineering.

My backend toolkit includes Java, Spring Boot and Spring Security, Python and Flask, REST APIs, and microservices. I also work with C/C++, JavaScript, and shell scripting where the problem calls for them.

RESEARCH DIRECTION

I am interested in the connection between software and physical systems: soft robotics, autonomous behavior, sensory systems, biosensors, and biomimetic modeling.

MY PHILOSOPHY

What does ChatGPT think about me?

A reflection on the projects, interests, and conversations I have shared.

Silver VS approaches engineering as a way to understand what happens beneath the interface. Getting something to work opens the next set of questions: why does it work, what assumptions hold it together, and how can those assumptions be tested?

That curiosity connects backend software, cryptography, reverse engineering, and bionic systems. Across those fields, the approach is similar: identify the mechanism, build a model, examine its limits, and compare the explanation with what can actually be observed.

He values the ability to inspect, modify, and maintain the tools he relies on. Personal tooling, automation, and self-hosting give him room to learn through ownership. Choosing an existing tool can be just as sound an engineering decision when it fits the problem.

His move from computing toward bionics brings those questions into the physical world. A biological analogy needs a defensible correspondence; a sensor reading needs calibration and context; a prototype needs evidence before its behavior becomes a conclusion.

This workbench reflects that way of learning. It leaves room for unfinished investigations, records the reasoning behind decisions, and connects what was built with what was learned. The aim is to make each explanation precise enough to challenge and each result clear enough for someone else to examine.
